items.title: The oxygen you breathe comes from WATER, not CO2
items.claim: Photosynthesis takes in CO2 and water and produces sugar and oxygen. Every chemistry student writes the equation. But the O2 released is not stripped from the CO2 — it comes entirely from splitting water molecules.
items.prompt: How do we know the oxygen comes from water?

options.text: Both water and CO2 contribute oxygen equally
Ruben and Kamen (1941) used the heavy isotope oxygen-18 to label either water or CO2; the released O2 carried the label only when the water was labelled, never when the CO2 was
CO2 is the source of the oxygen

items.reveal:
The light reactions of photosynthesis split water (photolysis) at the oxygen-evolving complex — a manganese-calcium cluster in Photosystem II. Two water molecules are split: 2 H2O -> 4 H+ + 4 e- + O2.

The electrons enter the electron transport chain. The protons contribute to the thylakoid pH gradient (lumen reaches pH ~5, stroma ~8). ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP.

The Calvin cycle (in the stroma) uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar. The carbon from CO2 becomes the carbon in glucose. But the oxygen atoms in CO2 mostly end up in carbohydrate, NOT in the released O2.

Oxygen is, from photosynthesis's point of view, a waste product — and arguably the most consequential pollution event in Earth's history (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago, killed most anaerobic life).
items.why: The arrow-pushing equation suggests CO2 donates oxygen. The actual chemistry inverts that: water is split, CO2 is reduced, and the oxygen you breathe was once dissolved in a chloroplast.

items.title: Reintroducing wolves changed the course of rivers in Yellowstone
items.claim: Grey wolves were exterminated from Yellowstone by 1926. In 1995, 14 wolves were reintroduced. Within 20 years, elk populations dropped, willows and aspen regrew along riverbanks, beaver populations rose, and river channels narrowed.

options.text: A trophic cascade: wolves reduce elk numbers and (especially) keep them moving, releasing browse pressure on streamside trees, which stabilise banks. The effect propagates through multiple trophic levels
Wolves drink large amounts of river water
It's coincidence — climate change did it

items.reveal:
The Yellowstone story is the textbook trophic cascade. Wolves don't only kill elk; they shift elk behaviour — herds avoid areas where they can't see predators coming, like valley bottoms with dense vegetation.

Released from constant browsing, willows and aspens regrow. Beavers, which need willows, return — by 2014, beaver colonies had increased from 1 to 9. Beaver dams trap sediment, raise water tables, create wetlands.

The full claim ('wolves changed the rivers') is contested. William Ripple and Robert Beschta documented the vegetation rebound; Arthur Middleton and others argue confounding factors (climate, bear predation, elk hunting outside the park) explain much of it.

What is uncontroversial: keystone species have effects on ecosystems vastly out of proportion to their biomass. Sea otters and kelp forests, starfish and intertidal communities, sharks and seagrass — similar cascades documented worldwide.

Keystone species concept: Robert Paine (1969), who removed starfish from a Pacific Northwest tide pool and watched it collapse to a mussel monoculture.
items.why: Ecosystems are imagined as bottom-up: plants determine herbivores determine carnivores. Top predators flip the picture — top-down control is real, and big effects can come from species with little biomass.

items.title: You are outnumbered by your own bacteria
items.claim: Adult humans carry about 38 trillion bacterial cells, roughly matching the count of human cells. By gene count, microbial DNA dwarfs human DNA by 100 to 1. They digest your food, train your immune system and affect your behaviour.

options.text: Humans have 10 times more bacteria than human cells
The ratio is closer to 1.3:1 (bacteria:human), based on revised counts (Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016) — much closer than the older 10:1 figure suggested
There are about as many bacterial cells as human red blood cells
Bacterial cell count is roughly the same as human muscle cell count

items.reveal:
The famous 10:1 ratio came from a 1972 back-of-envelope estimate by Thomas Luckey. It propagated through textbooks for 40 years.

In 2016, Sender, Fuchs and Milo revisited the numbers. They estimated about 30 trillion human cells (84 percent red blood cells) and 38 trillion bacterial cells (most in the colon). The ratio is close to 1:1.

Gene count is a different story. Each human cell carries 20,000 genes; the gut microbiome contains an estimated 2 to 20 million unique microbial genes — so by gene count, we're 99 percent microbe.

The gut microbiome makes vitamins, ferments fibre, modulates the immune system and produces neurotransmitters that may affect mood and behaviour (the 'gut-brain axis').
items.why: Self/other has clear boundaries in popular imagination. Biologically, the boundary is fuzzy and statistical.
